content: The detection rates of precancerous lesions may be slightly higher when using algorithms that incorporate dual-stain cytology for triage compared to those using cytology alone. However, these rates are lower when compared to algorithms employing other triage tests. The lifetime discounted costs of algorithms using dual-stain cytology for triage are comparable to those using cytology alone, assuming the costs of dual-stain cytology are similar to cytology. These costs are higher than those of algorithms using other triage tests. Based on these cost assumptions, the cost-effectiveness of dual-stain cytology for triage may be similar to other triage tests. A significant reduction in effectiveness was observed when compliance with follow-up at 24 months decreased from 90% to 70%. Most studies collected samples via health workers, and recommendations are based on this sampling method. Due to limited data on dual-stain cytology in women living with HIV, a separate analysis could not be conducted. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) agreed that the recommendations presented do not apply to women living with HIV. The GDG also evaluated the potential advantages of using dual-stain cytology for triage compared to other triage tests. Findings from surveys and systematic reviews on values, preferences, acceptability, feasibility, and equity were considered when formulating this recommendation. These findings were applied to dual-stain cytology based on evidence for cytology. Limited evidence specific to dual-stain cytology for triage testing was available. However, the GDG noted potential challenges in providing dual-stain cytology as a triage test in settings without liquid-based cytology (LBC) services that are quality-controlled and assured. The GDG emphasized the need for longitudinal data, with follow-up exceeding five years, to assess the impact of dual-stain cytology within cervical screening programs. Most studies have been conducted in high-income settings, highlighting the need for data generation in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), where diagnostic and treatment capacities may differ. Additional studies comparing the accuracy of self-collected versus health provider-collected samples are also necessary. Trials assessing the performance of dual-stain cytology in women living with HIV and comparing the screen-triage-treat approach using dual-stain cytology versus other triage tests are urgently needed. Research in LMIC settings is particularly important, given the differences in diagnostic and treatment capacities compared to high-income settings. Studies evaluating the long-term benefits and risks of different screening tests and strategies, including varying screening intervals and collection techniques, are essential. Implementation studies on screening and treatment strategies using dual-stain cytology for triage testing are also required. These studies should address the feasibility of dual-stain cytology, including training, infrastructure needs, and quality assurance, as well as its acceptability among stakeholders and its impact on accessibility and equity. The recommendation will be integrated into a consolidated version of the WHO guideline for screening and treating cervical precancerous lesions to prevent cervical cancer. This guideline will be disseminated through WHO’s global network to ensure accessibility for health workers and program managers. Dissemination strategies include publication on the WHO website, printed copies for health ministries, and translations into six official WHO languages. Regional workshops and webinars will support guideline adoption, implementation, and monitoring. The impact of the updated guideline will be assessed through surveys of health workers and clients one year after release to evaluate changes in country policies and national guidelines. This will also measure the guideline’s reach and its influence on clinical practice. Evidence on the sensitivity and specificity of different tests, including dual-stain cytology, is accumulating. Syntheses of this evidence will inform new recommendations as part of a “living guidelines” approach. The GDG will continue collaborating with the WHO Secretariat to address research gaps identified during the guideline development process.
